pos: v. (to twist by force; to pervert judgment or words; rendering Hebrew natah and atsab, Greek strebloo)
etymology: Old English wræstan, to twist. Peter's Greek, strebloo, is the rack — to wrest the Scriptures is to stretch them on it until they say what the torturer wants.
biblical_def: Peter on Paul's letters: “in which are some things hard to be understood, which they that are unlearned and unstable wrest, as they do also the other scriptures, unto their own destruction” (2Pe 3:16). The Law on judges: “Thou shalt not wrest judgment; thou shalt not respect persons, neither take a gift” (Deu 16:19); “Thou shalt not wrest the judgment of thy poor in his cause” (Exo 23:6); “neither shalt thou speak in a cause to decline after many to wrest judgment” (Exo 23:2). David: “Every day they wrest my words: all their thoughts are against me for evil” (Psa 56:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines wrest as to twist or extort by violence; to pull or force from by violent wringing or twisting; to distort; to turn from truth or twist from its natural meaning by violence.
webster_full: WREST, v.t. To twist or extort by violence; to pull or force from by violent wringing or twisting; as, to wrest an instrument from another's hands.
2. To take or force from by violence.
3. To distort; to turn from truth or twist from its natural meaning by violence; to pervert; as, to wrest the Scriptures.
scriptures: As also in all his epistles, speaking in them of these things; in which are some things hard to be understood, which they that are unlearned and unstable wrest, as they do also the other scriptures, unto their own destruction.
Thou shalt not wrest judgment; thou shalt not respect persons, neither take a gift: for a gift doth blind the eyes of the wise, and pervert the words of the righteous.
Exo 23:6
Thou shalt not wrest the judgment of thy poor in his cause.
Exo 23:2
Thou shalt not follow a multitude to do evil; neither shalt thou speak in a cause to decline after many to wrest judgment:
Psa 56:5
Every day they wrest my words: all their thoughts are against me for evil.
corruption_summary: Every cult is a wresting of Scripture, and Peter says it is done by the unlearned and unstable, which is a description of a method, not an insult.
corruption_paragraphs: Second Peter 3:16 gives the anatomy of false teaching in one sentence. Some things in Scripture are hard to be understood — Peter says so of Paul, an apostle of an apostle — and the hard places are where the wresting happens, because a difficult text can be stretched further than a plain one before it breaks. The wresters are the unlearned, who do not know the whole Bible and so cannot check the part, and the unstable, who have no fixed doctrine to be checked against. Every cult in history began with a hard text on the rack: a verse about baptism for the dead, a verse about the firstborn of every creature, a verse about the thousand years. The remedy is the Reformers' rule, that Scripture interprets Scripture and the plain governs the obscure — and Peter's closing word, that the wresting is unto their own destruction.

The Law's wresting is the courtroom's. A judge wrests judgment by turning it aside for a gift or a face, and Exodus 23 forbids the two ways it is done: bending toward the rich, and — the verse the modern reader misses — bending toward the poor because he is poor (v. 3, “neither shalt thou countenance a poor man in his cause”). Justice has no favourite class. Psalm 56:5 shows the same violence done to a man's words, twisted every day by enemies whose thoughts are against him; the Lord suffered it at His trial, and every honest man has had his sentences wrested since.
roots_summary: Hebrew natah (H5186), to turn aside, pervert; atsab (H6087), to twist, distort; Greek strebloo (G4761), to twist, torture on the rack.
roots_lines: Hebrew natah, hiphil (H5186) — to turn aside, wrest; Exodus 23:2, 23:6, Deuteronomy 16:19, 24:17, 27:19.
Hebrew atsab (H6087) — to twist, grieve, wrest; Psalm 56:5.
Greek strebloo (G4761) — to twist, rack, wrest; 2 Peter 3:16 only.
usage: “Which they that are unlearned and unstable wrest” — the rack, and who works it.
“Thou shalt not wrest judgment” — neither toward the rich nor toward the poor.
“Every day they wrest my words” — the Lord's trial, and every honest man's.

pos: v. and adj. (purified by fire, as metal; rendering Hebrew tsaraph and zaqaq)
etymology: Re + fine, to make fine again; the Hebrew tsaraph is the smelter's verb, and its participle is the refiner of Malachi 3.
biblical_def: God to Israel in Babylon: “Behold, I have refined thee, but not with silver; I have chosen thee in the furnace of affliction” (Isa 48:10). Zechariah's remnant: “I will bring the third part through the fire, and will refine them as silver is refined, and will try them as gold is tried: they shall call on my name, and I will hear them” (Zec 13:9). David gave for the temple “refined gold by weight” for the altar of incense (1Ch 28:18) and “seven thousand talents of refined silver, to overlay the walls” (1Ch 29:4). The feast on the mountain is “of wines on the lees well refined” (Isa 25:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines refined as purified; separated from extraneous matter; assayed, as metals; purified from what is coarse, rude, or vulgar.
webster_full: REFINED, pp. Purified; separated from extraneous matter; assayed, as metals; purified from what is coarse, rude or vulgar; polished; separated from what is gross.
scriptures: Behold, I have refined thee, but not with silver; I have chosen thee in the furnace of affliction.
Zec 13:9

And I will bring the third part through the fire, and will refine them as silver is refined, and will try them as gold is tried: they shall call on my name, and I will hear them: I will say, It is my people: and they shall say, The LORD is my God.
And for the altar of incense refined gold by weight; and gold for the pattern of the chariot of the cherubims, that spread out their wings, and covered the ark of the covenant of the LORD.
Even three thousand talents of gold, of the gold of Ophir, and seven thousand talents of refined silver, to overlay the walls of the houses withal:
Isa 25:6
And in this mountain shall the LORD of hosts make unto all people a feast of fat things, a feast of wines on the lees, of fat things full of marrow, of wines on the lees well refined.
corruption_summary: Affliction is read as the evidence of God's rejection, and Isaiah 48:10 says the furnace is where He chose you.
corruption_paragraphs: “I have refined thee, but not with silver” is God's explanation of the exile to the exiles, and the second clause is the one to hold: I have chosen thee in the furnace of affliction. The prosperity gospel reads suffering as the sign that something is wrong between the sufferer and God; Isaiah 48 reads it as the sign that God has taken the trouble to refine. Silver is refined in a crucible by a man who wants the silver; the dross is not refined, it is thrown away. The furnace is election's workshop. Zechariah 13:9 adds the outcome: the third part brought through the fire, refined as silver, calling on His name and heard — a remnant, smaller than it went in, and pure.

David's refined gold and silver were for the house of God, and the picture holds for the church. Nothing goes on the altar of incense or the temple walls until it has been through the fire; the Lord builds with refined material, and the refining is not a punishment for being metal but the condition of being used. Malachi 3:3 has Him sitting as a refiner and purifier of silver over the sons of Levi — sitting, because the refiner watches the crucible until he can see his own face in it, and then the fire is done.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsaraph (H6884), to smelt, refine, test; zaqaq (H2212), to strain, purify, refine.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsaraph (H6884) — to refine, try; Isaiah 48:10, Zechariah 13:9, Psalm 66:10, Malachi 3:2–3.
Hebrew zaqaq (H2212) — to purify, refine; 1 Chronicles 28:18, 29:4, Isaiah 25:6, Job 28:1, Malachi 3:3.
usage: “I have refined thee… I have chosen thee in the furnace of affliction” — election's workshop.
“Will refine them as silver is refined” — the third part, through the fire.
“Refined gold by weight” — nothing on the altar that has not been through the crucible.

pos: v. (spoiled, disfigured, ruined; rendering Hebrew mishchat and shachath, Greek apollumi)
etymology: Old English merran, to hinder, spoil. Isaiah's word for the Servant's face is a noun, disfigurement — a marring so complete it is no longer a man's.
biblical_def: Of the Servant: “As many were astonied at thee; his visage was so marred more than any man, and his form more than the sons of men” (Isa 52:14). At the potter's house: “the vessel that he made of clay was marred in the hand of the potter: so he made it again another vessel, as seemed good to the potter to make it” (Jer 18:4). The girdle at Euphrates “was marred, it was profitable for nothing” (Jer 13:7). New wine in old bottles: “the wine is spilled, and the bottles will be marred” (Mar 2:22). Of Israel: “the emptiers have emptied them out, and marred their vine branches” (Nah 2:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines marred as injured; spoiled; hurt; impaired; disfigured; defaced.
webster_full: MARRED, pp. Injured; spoiled; hurt; impaired; disfigured; defaced.
scriptures: As many were astonied at thee; his visage was so marred more than any man, and his form more than the sons of men:
Jer 18:4
And the vessel that he made of clay was marred in the hand of the potter: so he made it again another vessel, as seemed good to the potter to make it.
Jer 13:7
Then I went to Euphrates, and digged, and took the girdle from the place where I had hid it: and, behold, the girdle was marred, it was profitable for nothing.
Mar 2:22
And no man putteth new wine into old bottles: else the new wine doth burst the bottles, and the wine is spilled, and the bottles will be marred: but new wine must be put into new bottles.
Nah 2:2
For the LORD hath turned away the excellency of Jacob, as the excellency of Israel: for the emptiers have emptied them out, and marred their vine branches.
corruption_summary: The crucifix is painted serene, and Isaiah says the Servant's face was marred beyond any man's.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 52:14 is the verse the religious painters could not obey. The Servant's visage was marred more than any man — the Hebrew is a noun, disfigurement, as if the face had become a thing rather than a face — and His form more than the sons of men, so that those who saw Him were astonied. The serene Christ of the crucifix, composed and lightly wounded, is a denial of the text and of what the text means: that the wrath borne there was total and the body showed it. The verse stands at the head of the Servant song on purpose, so that the reader who comes to “he was wounded for our transgressions” already knows what wounded looked like. There is no gospel in a tidy cross.

Jeremiah 18:4 is about the potter's freedom, and it is usually preached about the clay's. The vessel was marred in the potter's hand, and he made it again another vessel — as seemed good to the potter. The sentimental reading makes the verse a promise that God will remake every broken life; the text's own application, in verse 6, is sovereignty: “as the clay is in the potter's hand, so are ye in mine hand, O house of Israel,” followed by God's right to pluck up or to build. The comfort in the chapter is real, and it is the comfort of being in that hand, not of having a claim on it.
roots_summary: Hebrew mishchat (H4893), disfigurement, corruption; shachath (H7843), to spoil, ruin, corrupt; Greek apollumi (G622), to destroy, ruin.
roots_lines: Hebrew mishchat (H4893) — disfigurement, marring; Isaiah 52:14 only.
Hebrew shachath (H7843) — to spoil, mar, corrupt; Jeremiah 13:7, 18:4, Nahum 2:2, Genesis 6:12.
Greek apollumi (G622) — to destroy, be marred; Mark 2:22, Luke 5:37.
usage: “His visage was so marred more than any man” — no gospel in a tidy cross.
“Marred in the hand of the potter: so he made it again” — the potter's freedom, not the clay's claim.
“The girdle was marred, it was profitable for nothing” — Judah at Euphrates.

pos: v. and adj. (established, settled, immovable; rendering Hebrew kun, Greek sterizo)
etymology: Latin fixus, fastened. The Hebrew of the Psalms is the word for a thing set up and established; the Greek of Luke 16 is the word for a thing made to stand fast.
biblical_def: David from the cave: “My heart is fixed, O God, my heart is fixed: I will sing and give praise” (Psa 57:7; Psa 108:1). Of the righteous man: “He shall not be afraid of evil tidings: his heart is fixed, trusting in the LORD” (Psa 112:7). And Abraham to the rich man: “beside all this, between us and you there is a great gulf fixed: so that they which would pass from hence to you cannot; neither can they pass to us, that would come from thence” (Luk 16:26).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines fixed as settled; established; firm; fast; stable.
webster_full: FIXED, pp. Settled; established; firm; fast; stable.
scriptures: Psa 57:7
My heart is fixed, O God, my heart is fixed: I will sing and give praise.
He shall not be afraid of evil tidings: his heart is fixed, trusting in the LORD.
And beside all this, between us and you there is a great gulf fixed: so that they which would pass from hence to you cannot; neither can they pass to us, that would come from thence.
A Song or Psalm of David. O God, my heart is fixed; I will sing and give praise, even with my glory.
corruption_summary: Purgatory and the second chance require a passage the Lord said was fixed shut, and the anxious age needs the heart Psalm 112 describes.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke 16:26 closes the door that purgatory, prayers for the dead, and the hope of a second chance all require to be open. Abraham's words to the rich man are not about the impossibility of mercy but about the fixity of the state: a great gulf, fixed, so that none can pass either way. The Lord who told the parable is the Judge who will fix the states, and He described the gulf as already set in the intermediate state, before the resurrection and the last judgment. Every doctrine of a post-mortem passage — from the Roman purgatory to the modern universalist's hope that hell will empty — has to cross a gulf the Lord said was fixed.

The Psalms' fixed heart is the answer to an anxious age. Psalm 112:7 is exact about the mechanism: the righteous man is not afraid of evil tidings because his heart is fixed, trusting in the LORD — the fear is not managed, it is displaced by a settledness that was in place before the news arrived. David wrote Psalm 57 in a cave with Saul outside, and the fixed heart sings there: my heart is fixed, I will sing and give praise. A heart fixed on God is not one that has stopped feeling; it is one that has decided in advance where its weight goes, so that the tidings, when they come, find it already leaning.
roots_summary: Hebrew kun (H3559), to be established, set up, fixed; Greek sterizo (G4741), to make fast, establish.
roots_lines: Hebrew kun, niphal (H3559) — established, fixed; Psalm 57:7, 108:1, 112:7, 51:10, “a right spirit.”
Greek sterizo (G4741) — to fix, establish; Luke 16:26, 9:51, Romans 1:11, 1 Peter 5:10.
usage: “A great gulf fixed” — the door purgatory needs, shut by the Lord.
“He shall not be afraid of evil tidings: his heart is fixed” — settled before the news.
“My heart is fixed, O God… I will sing” — from a cave, with Saul outside.

pos: n. and v. (provision for a want; to furnish what is lacking; rendering Greek pleroo, epichoregia, anapleroo, and husterema)
etymology: Latin supplere, to fill up. Every New Testament use of the word is about a lack met, and the last of them is the promise of Philippians 4:19.
biblical_def: “But my God shall supply all your need according to his riches in glory by Christ Jesus” (Php 4:19). Paul in prison: “I know that this shall turn to my salvation through your prayer, and the supply of the Spirit of Jesus Christ” (Php 1:19). Epaphroditus came near to death “to supply your lack of service toward me” (Php 2:30). And the rule of equality among churches: “that now at this time your abundance may be a supply for their want, that their abundance also may be a supply for your want” (2Co 8:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines supply as to fill up, as any deficiency happens; to furnish what is wanted; and, as a noun, sufficiency for wants given or furnished.
webster_full: SUPPLY, v.t. To fill up, as any deficiency happens; to furnish what is wanted; to afford or furnish a sufficiency.
2. To serve instead of.
SUPPLY, n. Sufficiency for wants given or furnished; that which is provided to fill up a deficiency.
scriptures: Php 4:19
But my God shall supply all your need according to his riches in glory by Christ Jesus.
Php 1:19
For I know that this shall turn to my salvation through your prayer, and the supply of the Spirit of Jesus Christ,
But by an equality, that now at this time your abundance may be a supply for their want, that their abundance also may be a supply for your want: that there may be equality:
Php 2:30
Because for the work of Christ he was nigh unto death, not regarding his life, to supply your lack of service toward me.
corruption_summary: All your need is preached as all your wants, and the promise was made to a church that had just given to the point of need.
corruption_paragraphs: Philippians 4:19 is a promise with a context, and the context is verse 18. The Philippians had sent Epaphroditus with a gift that met Paul's need in a Roman prison — “I have all, and abound: I am full” — and the promise that follows is to them: my God shall supply all your need, because you have supplied mine. The verse is not a general guarantee of comfort; it is a specific assurance to givers who have given themselves into want that the God they gave for will not leave them there. The measure is “according to his riches in glory by Christ Jesus,” which is not a promise of riches but of a supply proportioned to an infinite source. And the word is need, which Paul had just distinguished from abundance in verse 12: he had learned both to be full and to be hungry, and the God who supplies need does not thereby promise never to teach the second lesson.

Second Corinthians 8:14 gives the mechanism by which the supply usually comes. Abundance in one church is a supply for want in another, and the roles reverse in time — an equality, Paul calls it, and he grounds it in the manna: he that gathered much had nothing over, and he that gathered little had no lack. The supply of God's people is mostly delivered through God's people, and the church that will not be the channel should not expect to be the destination.
roots_summary: Greek pleroo (G4137), to fill, supply; epichoregia (G2024), a furnishing, supply; anapleroo (G378), to fill up; husterema (G5303), a lack, want.
roots_lines: Greek pleroo (G4137) — to fill, supply; Philippians 4:19.
Greek epichoregia (G2024) — a supply, provision; Philippians 1:19, Ephesians 4:16.
Greek anapleroo (G378) — to fill up; Philippians 2:30; husterema (G5303), want, lack; 2 Corinthians 8:14, 9:12.
usage: “My God shall supply all your need” — said to givers who had given into want.
“The supply of the Spirit of Jesus Christ” — Paul's provision in prison.
“Your abundance may be a supply for their want” — the channel and the destination.

pos: adj. (acid, unripe, turned; rendering Hebrew boser, an unripe grape)
etymology: Old English sūr. The Hebrew behind the sour grape is the unripe grape, the one that sets the teeth on edge — and the proverb built on it was the exiles' excuse.
biblical_def: The proverb of the exile: “What mean ye, that ye use this proverb concerning the land of Israel, saying, The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge?” (Eze 18:2). Jeremiah promises its end: “In those days they shall say no more, The fathers have eaten a sour grape, and the children's teeth are set on edge. But every one shall die for his own iniquity: every man that eateth the sour grape, his teeth shall be set on edge” (Jer 31:29–30). Isaiah: “afore the harvest, when the bud is perfect, and the sour grape is ripening in the flower, he shall both cut off the sprigs” (Isa 18:5). Hosea: “Their drink is sour: they have committed whoredom continually” (Hos 4:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sour as acid; having a pungent taste; tart; crabbed; peevish; and, of things, turned, as milk.
webster_full: SOUR, a. Acid; having a pungent taste; sharp to the taste; tart; as, vinegar is sour; sour cider; sour beer.
2. Acid and austere or astringent; as, sour fruit.
3. Harsh of temper; crabbed; peevish; austere; morose.
4. Turned, as milk; rancid; musty.
scriptures: Eze 18:2
What mean ye, that ye use this proverb concerning the land of Israel, saying, The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge?
In those days they shall say no more, The fathers have eaten a sour grape, and the children's teeth are set on edge.
But every one shall die for his own iniquity: every man that eateth the sour grape, his teeth shall be set on edge.
Isa 18:5
For afore the harvest, when the bud is perfect, and the sour grape is ripening in the flower, he shall both cut off the sprigs with pruning hooks, and take away and cut down the branches.
Hos 4:18
Their drink is sour: they have committed whoredom continually: her rulers with shame do love, Give ye.
corruption_summary: Ezekiel 18 is used to deny original sin, and the exiles used the sour grape to deny their own, and the chapter answers both.
corruption_paragraphs: The exiles had a proverb that made their suffering their fathers' fault: the fathers ate the sour grape, and our teeth are set on edge. Ezekiel 18 takes the proverb away — the soul that sinneth, it shall die — and the chapter is a courtroom in which each generation is tried for its own deeds, so that no one in Babylon could plead Manasseh. That is the point, and it has been stretched to another: that Ezekiel denies the imputation of Adam's sin, since God judges each man only for what he himself has done. But Ezekiel is answering a proverb about temporal judgment on a nation, not writing Romans 5, and the same prophet who says the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father says the whole house of Israel has a heart of stone that must be replaced. Every man in the chapter is a sinner before the trial begins. What Ezekiel removes is the excuse, not the doctrine.

The teeth set on edge are the exile's own; the reader is meant to feel them. Jeremiah 31 sets the proverb's death beside the new covenant, four verses later — the law written in the heart, the sins remembered no more — because the man who stops blaming his fathers and owns his own sour grape is the man the new covenant is for. Personal responsibility is not the enemy of grace; it is its doorway.
roots_summary: Hebrew boser (H1155), an unripe, sour grape; sur (H5493), turned aside, of drink gone sour.
roots_lines: Hebrew boser (H1155) — unripe grape, sour grape; Isaiah 18:5, Jeremiah 31:29–30, Ezekiel 18:2, Job 15:33.
Hebrew sar (H5493) — turned, gone sour; Hosea 4:18.
usage: “The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge” — the exiles' excuse, taken away.
“Every man that eateth the sour grape, his teeth shall be set on edge” — and then the new covenant.
“Their drink is sour” — Hosea's Ephraim.

pos: n. (the upper side; in the AV only in upside down, overturned; rendering Hebrew haphak, avath, and hephek, Greek anastatoo)
etymology: Up + side. The phrase upside down is an overturning — a dish wiped and inverted, a world set on its head.
biblical_def: Of Jerusalem: “I will wipe Jerusalem as a man wipeth a dish, wiping it, and turning it upside down” (2Ki 21:13). Of the wicked: “the way of the wicked he turneth upside down” (Psa 146:9). Of the earth: “the LORD maketh the earth empty, and maketh it waste, and turneth it upside down” (Isa 24:1). Of the clay against the potter: “Surely your turning of things upside down shall be esteemed as the potter's clay: for shall the work say of him that made it, He made me not?” (Isa 29:16). And of the apostles at Thessalonica: “These that have turned the world upside down are come hither also” (Act 17:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines upside down as with the upper part undermost; in complete disorder.
webster_full: UPSIDE DOWN, adv. With the upper part undermost; hence, in complete disorder.
scriptures: Act 17:6
And when they found them not, they drew Jason and certain brethren unto the rulers of the city, crying, These that have turned the world upside down are come hither also;

Surely your turning of things upside down shall be esteemed as the potter's clay: for shall the work say of him that made it, He made me not? or shall the thing framed say of him that framed it, He had no understanding?
The LORD preserveth the strangers; he relieveth the fatherless and widow: but the way of the wicked he turneth upside down.
And I will stretch over Jerusalem the line of Samaria, and the plummet of the house of Ahab: and I will wipe Jerusalem as a man wipeth a dish, wiping it, and turning it upside down.
Isa 24:1
Behold, the LORD maketh the earth empty, and maketh it waste, and turneth it upside down, and scattereth abroad the inhabitants thereof.
corruption_summary: Turned the world upside down is quoted for Christian activism, and the charge at Thessalonica was that the apostles preached another King.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 17:6 is the church's favourite compliment, and it was an indictment. The men who dragged Jason before the rulers completed the sentence in the next verse: “these all do contrary to the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, one Jesus.” The world was turned upside down by a proclamation, not a programme — by the announcement that a crucified Jew was King and Caesar was not — and the disorder the city complained of was what that announcement does to every arrangement built on the other assumption. The church that wants to turn the world upside down by activism has kept the phrase and dropped the King, and the world, noticing, is not upset.

Isaiah 29:16 names the upside down that God Himself objects to: the clay judging the potter. “Your turning of things upside down” is the creature's verdict on the Creator — He made me not, He hath no understanding — and it is esteemed as the potter's clay, which is to say as nothing. Psalm 146:9 and 2 Kings 21:13 are the answer in kind: the way of the wicked God turneth upside down, and Jerusalem He wipes as a dish and inverts. There are two overturnings in Scripture, the creature's against God and God's against the creature, and only one of them holds.
roots_summary: Hebrew haphak (H2015), to turn, overturn; avath (H5791), to bend, pervert, subvert; avah (H5753), to distort; hephek (H2017), a turning upside down; Greek anastatoo (G387), to unsettle, upset.
roots_lines: Hebrew haphak (H2015) — to overturn; 2 Kings 21:13; avah (H5753), Isaiah 24:1; avath (H5791), Psalm 146:9.
Hebrew hephek (H2017) — perversity, turning upside down; Isaiah 29:16 only.
Greek anastatoo (G387) — to upset, turn upside down; Acts 17:6, 21:38, Galatians 5:12.
usage: “These that have turned the world upside down” — an indictment, completed by another king, one Jesus.
“Your turning of things upside down shall be esteemed as the potter's clay” — the creature's verdict on the Creator.
“Wiping it, and turning it upside down” — Jerusalem as a dish.

pos: v. (rejected after examination; refused permission; rendering Greek apodokimazo, Hebrew nu)
etymology: Dis + allow, from Old French alouer, to approve. Peter's Greek is the builder's verb: a stone tested and thrown out of the course.
biblical_def: Peter of Christ: “To whom coming, as unto a living stone, disallowed indeed of men, but chosen of God, and precious” (1Pe 2:4); “Unto you therefore which believe he is precious: but unto them which be disobedient, the stone which the builders disallowed, the same is made the head of the corner” (1Pe 2:7). The Law of vows: if a father “disallow her in the day that he heareth,” a daughter's vow does not stand, “and the LORD shall forgive her” (Num 30:5); if a husband “disallowed her on the day that he heard it,” the vow is void (Num 30:8); and if he “held his peace at her, and disallowed her not: then all her vows shall stand” (Num 30:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines disallow as to refuse permission, to deny the authority of; to reject; to disapprove.
webster_full: DISALLOW, v.t. To refuse permission, or not to permit; not to grant or authorize; as, to disallow a claim.
2. Not to approve; not to receive; to reject; as, to disallow a doctrine.
3. To testify dislike or disapprobation.
scriptures: To whom coming, as unto a living stone, disallowed indeed of men, but chosen of God, and precious,
Unto you therefore which believe he is precious: but unto them which be disobedient, the stone which the builders disallowed, the same is made the head of the corner,
Num 30:5

But if her father disallow her in the day that he heareth; not any of her vows, or of her bonds wherewith she hath bound her soul, shall stand: and the LORD shall forgive her, because her father disallowed her.
Num 30:8

But if her husband disallowed her on the day that he heard it; then he shall make her vow which she vowed, and that which she uttered with her lips, wherewith she bound her soul, of none effect: and the LORD shall forgive her.
And her husband heard it, and held his peace at her, and disallowed her not: then all her vows shall stand, and every bond wherewith she bound her soul shall stand.
corruption_summary: The church takes the builders' verdict for God's, and Numbers 30 gives a husband a power the age has voted out of existence.
corruption_paragraphs: The stone was disallowed by the builders — the men whose trade was stones, whose judgment was professional, whose verdict was unanimous — and God made it the head of the corner. Peter is quoting Psalm 118 and applying it to the Sanhedrin, and the principle outlives them: the considered rejection of Christ by the qualified is the normal course of history, and the church that adjusts its Christ to win their approval has joined the builders. He is precious to them that believe and a stone of stumbling to the disobedient, and there is no third stone.

Numbers 30 gives a father over his daughter's vow and a husband over his wife's the power to disallow, on the day he hears it, and the vow made in her rashness is void — and the LORD shall forgive her. The passage is headship in its gentlest form: a covering under which a woman's hasty word does not bind her, because a man answerable for her has said no. The age has abolished the arrangement as an insult and kept the rash vows. Verse 11 is the other side of the same headship: the husband who holds his peace has allowed, and the vow stands; silence is a decision, and a man cannot decline to be the head of what he has been made the head of.
roots_summary: Greek apodokimazo (G593), to reject after testing, disallow; Hebrew nu (H5106), to hinder, forbid, disallow.
roots_lines: Greek apodokimazo (G593) — to reject as unfit, disallow; 1 Peter 2:4, 2:7, Matthew 21:42, Luke 17:25, Hebrews 12:17.
Hebrew nu, hiphil (H5106) — to forbid, disallow; Numbers 30:5, 30:8, 30:11, 32:7.
usage: “Disallowed indeed of men, but chosen of God” — the builders' verdict and the Owner's.
“If her father disallow her… the LORD shall forgive her” — headship as a covering.
“Held his peace at her, and disallowed her not” — silence is a decision.

pos: adj. (in the AV, living, alive, vigorous; rendering Greek zao, participle, Hebrew chayeh and chai)
etymology: Life + ly, in the old sense of living. The modern word means animated; the Authorized Version's means alive, and Peter's lively hope is a living one.
biblical_def: Peter: God “hath begotten us again unto a lively hope by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead” (1Pe 1:3); and “Ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house, an holy priesthood” (1Pe 2:5). Stephen of Moses: “who received the lively oracles to give unto us” (Act 7:38). The midwives to Pharaoh: the Hebrew women “are lively, and are delivered ere the midwives come in unto them” (Exo 1:19). David: “mine enemies are lively, and they are strong” (Psa 38:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines lively as brisk, vigorous, active; gay, airy; representing life; strong, energetic; and, in Scripture, living, as lively stones.
webster_full: LIVELY, a. Brisk; vigorous; vivacious; active; as a lively youth.
2. Gay; airy.
3. Representing life; as a lively imitation of nature.
4. Strong; energetic; as a lively faith or hope; a lively persuasion.
scriptures: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, which according to his abundant mercy hath begotten us again unto a lively hope by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead,
Ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house, an holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God by Jesus Christ.
Act 7:38
This is he, that was in the church in the wilderness with the angel which spake to him in the mount Sina, and with our fathers: who received the lively oracles to give unto us:
Exo 1:19
And the midwives said unto Pharaoh, Because the Hebrew women are not as the Egyptian women; for they are lively, and are delivered ere the midwives come in unto them.
But mine enemies are lively, and they are strong: and they that hate me wrongfully are multiplied.
corruption_summary: The lively hope is read as a cheerful one, and Peter's word is living, because it comes by a resurrection.
corruption_paragraphs: Three of the New Testament's five uses of the word are Peter's and Stephen's, and in all three the Greek is the participle of to live: a living hope, living stones, living oracles. The modern reader hears lively as animated and misses the doctrine. The hope is living because it was begotten by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead — it is not a mood the believer works up but a life that was put in him — and it does not fade with the believer's spirits, because it is anchored in an empty tomb and not in him. The stones are living because the Stone they are laid on is (v. 4), and a church is a house of living stones or it is a quarry.

Stephen's lively oracles are the sharpest of the three. The law Moses received at Sinai is called living — not a dead letter, not a code superseded, but oracles with life in them — and Stephen said so to the council that was about to stone him for allegedly speaking against Moses. Hebrews 4:12 makes the same claim of the whole word: quick, which is the AV's other word for alive, and powerful. A Bible read as a dead book will be a dead book to the reader; Stephen's word for it is the word for the God who gave it.
roots_summary: Greek zao (G2198), participle, living; Hebrew chayeh (H2422), vigorous, lively; chai (H2416), living, vigorous.
roots_lines: Greek zao (G2198), participle — living, lively; 1 Peter 1:3, 2:4–5, Acts 7:38, Hebrews 4:12.
Hebrew chayeh (H2422) — vigorous; Exodus 1:19 only; chai (H2416), living, lively; Psalm 38:19.
usage: “A lively hope by the resurrection of Jesus Christ” — living, not cheerful.
“Ye also, as lively stones” — a house, or a quarry.
“The lively oracles” — Stephen on the law, to the men about to stone him.

pos: n. (one of the bones enclosing the chest; in Genesis, the side from which the woman was built; rendering Hebrew tsela and chomesh, Aramaic ala)
etymology: Old English ribb. The Hebrew of Genesis 2 is tsela, a side — the word used everywhere else for the side of the ark, the side of the tabernacle, the side of a hill.
biblical_def: “And the LORD God caused a deep sleep to fall upon Adam, and he slept: and he took one of his ribs, and closed up the flesh instead thereof; And the rib, which the LORD God had taken from man, made he a woman, and brought her unto the man” (Gen 2:21–22). The other rib is Joab's: Abner smote Asahel “under the fifth rib” (2Sa 2:23); Joab took Abner aside in the gate “and smote him there under the fifth rib” (2Sa 3:27), and Amasa, with a kiss, “in the fifth rib” (2Sa 20:10). Daniel's bear had “three ribs in the mouth of it” (Dan 7:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines rib as a bone of the side; one of the bones which enclose the thorax; also, in ship-building, a piece of timber which forms the side.
webster_full: RIB, n. A bone of animals which forms a part of the frame of the thorax. The ribs in the human body are twelve on each side, extending from the spine to the sternum.
2. In ship-building, a piece of timber which forms or strengthens the side of a ship.
3. Something long, thin and narrow; a strip.
scriptures: Gen 2:22
And the rib, which the LORD God had taken from man, made he a woman, and brought her unto the man.
Gen 2:21
And the LORD God caused a deep sleep to fall upon Adam, and he slept: and he took one of his ribs, and closed up the flesh instead thereof;
And when Abner was returned to Hebron, Joab took him aside in the gate to speak with him quietly, and smote him there under the fifth rib, that he died, for the blood of Asahel his brother.

But Amasa took no heed to the sword that was in Joab's hand: so he smote him therewith in the fifth rib, and shed out his bowels to the ground, and struck him not again; and he died. So Joab and Abishai his brother pursued after Sheba the son of Bichri.
Dan 7:5

And behold another beast, a second, like to a bear, and it raised up itself on one side, and it had three ribs in the mouth of it between the teeth of it: and they said thus unto it, Arise, devour much flesh.
corruption_summary: The rib is mocked as a fable and its order dismissed as culture, and Paul built the order of the church on the order of the rib.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 2:22 is the founding text of marriage, and the age treats it as the least believable verse in the Bible. Paul treated it as history with consequences: “For Adam was first formed, then Eve” (1Ti 2:13) is his reason for the order of the church, and “the man is not of the woman; but the woman of the man” (1Co 11:8) is his reason for the order of the home. The complementarian position is not a preference for an old arrangement; it is the apostle's exegesis of a rib. Matthew Henry's line has never been bettered — not made out of his head to top him, nor out of his feet to be trampled upon by him, but out of his side to be equal with him, under his arm to be protected, and near his heart to be beloved — and every word of it is a reading of where the bone came from.

The Hebrew is side, and the deep sleep is the first surgery; the woman was built (the verb is a builder's) from what was taken out of the man's side while he slept and could contribute nothing, which is the pattern of grace. The church has always seen the second Adam in it: from the side of the Man who slept on the cross came the water and the blood by which His bride is made. The fifth rib is the Bible's other use of the bone, and it is Joab's — three men killed there, one with a kiss — so that the same word marks the place a wife came from and the place a treacherous friend puts the knife.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsela (H6763), a rib, a side; chomesh (H2570), the fifth rib, the abdomen; Aramaic ala (H5967), a rib.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsela (H6763) — rib, side; Genesis 2:21–22, Exodus 25:12, 26:20, 2 Samuel 16:13.
Hebrew chomesh (H2570) — the fifth rib, belly; 2 Samuel 2:23, 3:27, 4:6, 20:10.
Aramaic ala (H5967) — rib; Daniel 7:5 only.
usage: “The rib, which the LORD God had taken from man, made he a woman” — Paul's exegesis of it is the order of the church.
“Out of his side to be equal with him, under his arm to be protected, near his heart to be beloved” — Henry on the bone.
“Smote him there under the fifth rib” — Joab's word for the same bone.
